sections.content: Every house flip starts with a number. Get it right, and you walk away with a check. Get it wrong, and you could lose tens of thousands of dollars on a single deal. That is why smart investors always run the numbers before they make an offer — and why a free house flip profit calculator is one of the most valuable tools in your arsenal.

Whether you are brand new to flipping or you have closed dozens of deals, this guide will walk you through exactly how to calculate your potential profit, which costs most beginners forget, and how to use free tools to do the math fast and accurately.
What Is a House Flip Profit Calculator?

A house flip profit calculator is a tool that helps you estimate your net profit from a fix-and-flip deal before you buy. You plug in the numbers — purchase price, repair costs, holding costs, selling costs, and the after repair value (ARV) — and the calculator spits out your estimated profit and return on investment. The goal is simple: know your numbers before you commit your money.
"The money is made when you buy, not when you sell." — A fundamental principle every real estate investor needs to internalize before making their first offer.
The Core Formula Every House Flipper Needs to Know
Before you touch any calculator, you need to understand the basic profit formula. This is the foundation everything else is built on:

items: Net Profit = ARV − Purchase Price − Rehab Costs − Holding Costs − Selling Costs − Financing Costs
ARV (After Repair Value): What the property will sell for after all renovations are complete
Purchase Price: What you pay for the property, including any assignment fees or closing costs to acquire it
Rehab Costs: The full cost of all repairs, renovations, and updates
Holding Costs: Monthly expenses while you own the property (taxes, insurance, utilities, HOA)
Selling Costs: Agent commissions (typically 5–6%), transfer taxes, closing costs (1–2%)
Financing Costs: Hard money interest, loan origination fees, or opportunity cost on cash

sections.content: A Real-World Example: Running the Numbers on a $180,000 Deal
Let's say you find a distressed property in a neighborhood where comparable homes sell for $275,000 after renovation. Here is how the numbers might break down:

items: Purchase Price: $155,000
Rehab Costs: $45,000 (kitchen, bathrooms, roof, paint, flooring)
Holding Costs: $4,200 (6 months × $700/month for taxes, insurance, utilities)
Selling Costs: $19,250 (7% of $275,000 for agent commissions + closing costs)
Financing Costs: $6,500 (hard money loan at 12% interest for 6 months)
Total Costs: $229,950

sections.content: That is a solid flip. But notice that the profit is not just ARV minus purchase price. If you had skipped the other cost categories, you might have thought this deal would net $120,000. The full picture matters enormously — and that is exactly what a good flip profit calculator forces you to see.

Pro Tip: Always add a 10–15% contingency buffer on top of your rehab estimate. Unexpected costs — rotted subfloor, outdated electrical, hidden plumbing issues — show up on almost every flip. Build the cushion in before you make your offer, not after.
The Costs Most Beginners Forget

Newcomers to flipping often underestimate how many line items eat into their profit. If you are just getting started, the [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) is a great place to build your foundational knowledge. In the meantime, here are the most commonly missed costs in a flip calculation:

items: Permit fees: Can range from $500 to $5,000+ depending on your city and the scope of work
Staging costs: Professional staging can cost $1,500–$4,000 but often increases your sale price
Carrying costs during delays: If your flip takes 10 months instead of 6, your holding costs jump significantly
Buyer concessions: In slower markets, you may need to cover 1–3% of the buyer's closing costs
Capital gains taxes: Short-term capital gains (properties held under 1 year) are taxed as ordinary income — often 22–37%
Loan origination fees: Most hard money lenders charge 1–3 points upfront on the loan amount

sections.content: How to Use a Free House Flip Profit Calculator Effectively
Step 1: Get an Accurate ARV

Your ARV is the most important number in the entire calculation. Pull recent sold comps — homes that sold within the last 3–6 months, within half a mile, with similar square footage and bed/bath count. A bad ARV estimate can make a terrible deal look great on paper.
Step 2: Estimate Rehab Costs Accurately

Walk the property with a contractor or use a structured scope of work. You can get a fast starting point with the free [Rehab Estimator at aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator), which helps you itemize renovation costs room by room. Never guess on rehab — it is the number that kills more deals than anything else.
Step 3: Map Out Your Holding Period

How long will you own the property? A realistic timeline accounts for acquisition (2–4 weeks), renovation (2–5 months), listing and sale (1–3 months), and closing (30–45 days). Add these up and multiply by your monthly holding costs. Even a two-month delay can cost you $3,000–$6,000 in a typical market.
Step 4: Add All Selling and Financing Costs

Budget 6–8% of your ARV for selling costs (realtor commissions, title fees, transfer taxes). If you are using a hard money loan, calculate the total interest and points for your entire projected hold period, not just a few months.
What Profit Margin Should You Target on a Flip?

Most experienced flippers aim for a minimum net profit of $20,000 per deal, or at least a 15–20% return on total investment. In competitive markets, margins have compressed — which makes your pre-purchase analysis even more critical. Deals that look thin on paper often become money-losers when unexpected costs hit.

In high-volume markets like [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), the competition for distressed properties is intense. Running tight, accurate numbers is how you stay profitable when other investors are overpaying. You can explore active deal flow in these markets directly through AIWholesail to find properties already pre-screened for flip potential.
The 70% Rule: A Quick Sanity Check

The 70% rule is a shorthand formula used by house flippers as a quick filter before doing a full analysis. The formula is: Maximum Purchase Price = (ARV × 70%) − Rehab Costs. Using our earlier example: ($275,000 × 0.70) − $45,000 = $147,500. That gives you a rough ceiling for what you should pay. The 70% rule does not replace a full profit calculator, but it helps you quickly eliminate deals that are obviously overpriced.

Pro Tip: The 70% rule works best in markets with stable values and predictable rehab costs. In hot or volatile markets, some investors use 65% to leave extra margin for error. Adjust the rule based on your local market conditions and experience level.
Flipping vs. Wholesaling: Know When to Pass the Deal

Sometimes a deal is not right for flipping but is still a great opportunity. If your profit calculator shows thin margins — say, under $15,000 — the property might make more sense to wholesale to another investor for a quick assignment fee.
